tips.title: Bronze has tin, brass has zinc
tips.body: Both are **copper** alloys. **Bronze** is copper and **tin**; **brass** is copper and **zinc**. A way to keep them apart: bron**z**e sounds like zinc but is not — it is the **t**in one, and brass is the **z**inc one.

tips.title: Carats are twenty-fourths
tips.body: **24 carat is pure gold**, so a carat is $\frac{1}{24}$. **18 carat** is $\frac{18}{24} = 75\%$ gold; **9 carat** is $\frac{9}{24} = 37.5\%$. Divide by 24 and multiply by 100.

tips.title: Carbon content decides the steel
tips.body: **High** carbon steel is **strong but brittle**; **low** carbon steel is **softer and more easily shaped**. Add **chromium and nickel** and you get **stainless steel** — hard and **resistant to corrosion**. The amount of carbon is the variable that changes everything.

tips.title: Thermosetting does not melt
tips.body: **Thermosoftening** polymers **melt when heated**; **thermosetting** polymers **do not**. The reason is structural: thermosetting polymers have **cross-links** holding the chains together, so heating cannot separate them.

tips.title: A composite is two materials
tips.body: Most composites are **two materials**: a **matrix or binder** surrounding and binding **fibres or fragments** of the other material, called the **reinforcement**. Concrete, fibreglass and wood all fit that pattern.

steps.title: Alloys in everyday use
steps.body:
**Most metals in everyday use are alloys** — mixtures of a metal with other elements. You already know *why* alloys are harder than pure metals: the different-sized atoms **distort the layers** so they cannot slide over one another. This topic is about **which alloys** and **what they are for**.

**Bronze** is an alloy of **copper and tin**, used for **statues, bells and ship propellers**.

**Brass** is an alloy of **copper and zinc**, used for **musical instruments, taps and door fittings**.

**Gold** used as jewellery is usually an alloy with **silver, copper and zinc**, because pure gold is too soft to wear. The proportion of gold is measured in **carats**: **24 carat is 100%** — pure gold — and **18 carat is 75% gold**.

**Aluminium alloys are low density**, which is why they are used where weight matters, such as in aircraft.

**Steels** are alloys of **iron** containing **specific amounts of carbon and other metals**, and the amount of carbon changes the properties completely:

- **High carbon steel** is **strong but brittle**, so it is used for **cutting tools and blades**.
- **Low carbon steel** is **softer and more easily shaped**, so it is used for **car bodies and sheeting**.
- Steels containing **chromium and nickel** — **stainless steels** — are **hard and resistant to corrosion**, so they are used for **cutlery and sinks**.

steps.title: Glass and clay ceramics
steps.body:
**Most of the glass we use is soda-lime glass**, made by **heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate, limestone**. It is cheap and suits bottles, windows and jars.

**Borosilicate glass** is made from **sand and boron trioxide**. It **melts at higher temperatures** than soda-lime glass, which is why it is used for laboratory glassware and ovenware — it survives heating that would soften ordinary glass.

Notice that **both start from sand**. The difference is what is added: sodium carbonate and limestone for one, boron trioxide for the other.

**Clay ceramics**, including **pottery and bricks**, are made by **shaping wet clay and then heating it in a furnace**. The heating drives out water and causes chemical changes that make the shape permanent and hard.

**Ceramics in general** are hard, stiff and brittle, resist heat and do not conduct electricity — which is why they are used for insulators, crockery and building materials.

steps.title: Polymers and composites
steps.body:
**The properties of polymers depend on what monomers they are made from and the conditions under which they are made.**

The clearest example is that **low density (LD) and high density (HD) poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene** — the *same* monomer. Different **catalysts, temperatures and pressures** give chains that pack differently: LD poly(ethene) is flexible and used for bags, HD poly(ethene) is more rigid and used for bottles and pipes.

**Two kinds of polymer, by what heating does:**

- **Thermosoftening polymers melt when they are heated.** Their chains are **separate**, held together only by weak forces, so heating lets them slide apart. They can be melted and reshaped repeatedly, which makes them easy to recycle.
- **Thermosetting polymers do not melt when they are heated.** Their chains are joined by strong **cross-links** — covalent bonds between the chains — forming a single rigid network. Heating cannot separate them, so the polymer keeps its shape and eventually chars instead of melting.

**Composites.** **Most composites are made of two materials: a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of the other material, which is called the reinforcement.**

The point is that the combination has properties **neither material has alone**: concrete is strong in compression because of the aggregate and holds together because of the cement.

boxes.title: Thermosetting

boxes.title: Why it matters

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Keep bronze and brass apart.** Bronze is copper and **tin**; brass is copper and **zinc**. Both are copper alloys, and mixing them up is the commonest single error in this topic.

**Give a use with a reason.** "High carbon steel is used for blades" is worth less than "used for blades **because it is hard and strong**, and its brittleness matters less in a tool that is not bent". The property should justify the use.

**Explain stainless steel by its additives.** **Chromium and nickel** make it hard and **resistant to corrosion**, which is why it suits cutlery, sinks and chemical plant — places that are constantly wet.

**Divide by 24 for carats.** $\frac{18}{24} = 75\%$, $\frac{9}{24} = 37.5\%$. Treating a carat as a percentage directly is wrong.

**Say why borosilicate is used where it is.** It **melts at a higher temperature** than soda-lime glass, so it survives heating — laboratory glassware and ovenware. The property drives the application.

**Explain the polymer difference structurally.** Thermosoftening chains are **separate**, held by weak forces, so they slide apart on heating. Thermosetting chains are joined by **cross-links**, which are covalent and do not break on heating. Naming cross-links is what earns the mark.

**Attribute LD and HD poly(ethene) to conditions.** Same **monomer**, different **catalyst, temperature and pressure** — so the answer is never "different monomers".

**Identify both parts of a composite.** Name the **matrix or binder** and the **reinforcement** separately, and say that the combination has properties neither has alone.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Most metals in everyday use are alloys.**
- **Bronze** = **copper and tin**; **brass** = **copper and zinc**.
- **Gold jewellery** is gold alloyed with **silver, copper and zinc**; purity is measured in **carats**, with **24 carat = 100%** and **18 carat = 75%**.
- **Steels** are alloys of **iron** with **specific amounts of carbon and other metals**.
- **High carbon steel**: **strong but brittle** — cutting tools.
- **Low carbon steel**: **softer and more easily shaped** — car bodies.
- **Stainless steel** contains **chromium and nickel**: **hard and corrosion resistant** — cutlery and sinks.
- **Aluminium alloys** are **low density** — aircraft.
- **Soda-lime glass**: heat **sand, sodium carbonate, limestone**.
- **Borosilicate glass**: **sand and boron trioxide**; **melts at higher temperatures**.
- **Clay ceramics**: **shape wet clay, then heat in a furnace**.
- Polymer properties depend on the **monomers** and the **conditions**; LD and HD poly(ethene) both come from **ethene**.
- **Thermosoftening melts** when heated; **thermosetting does not**, because of **cross-links**.
- A **composite** is a **matrix or binder** surrounding **fibres or fragments** of a **reinforcement**.

questions.prompt: Explain why thermosetting polymers do not melt when heated.
questions.solution:
Thermosetting polymers have **cross-links** — **covalent bonds between the chains** — which join them into a **single giant network**.

Heating gives the chains more energy, but the cross-links are **strong covalent bonds** that the heat cannot break, so the chains **cannot slide apart**. The polymer keeps its shape and eventually chars rather than melting.

Thermosoftening polymers have **separate chains** held only by **weak intermolecular forces**, which heating easily overcomes — so they melt.

questions.prompt:
A manufacturer is choosing materials for a new range of kitchen products: a set of knives, a sink, a set of measuring jugs that will go in the oven, and flexible food bags.

Recommend a suitable material for each, justifying your choices in terms of properties. (6 marks)
questions.solution:
**Knives: high carbon steel.** Steels are alloys of iron containing **specific amounts of carbon**, and a **high** carbon content makes the steel **strong and hard**, so it takes and holds a sharp cutting edge. It is **brittle**, but a blade is not meant to bend, so that drawback does not matter here.

**Sink: stainless steel.** A sink is **constantly wet**, so rusting would be the main risk. Steels containing **chromium and nickel** are **hard and resistant to corrosion**, which is exactly the requirement, and the hardness resists scratching from pans.

**Oven jugs: borosilicate glass.** Most glass is **soda-lime glass**, made from sand, sodium carbonate and limestone, but it softens at relatively low temperatures. **Borosilicate glass**, made from **sand and boron trioxide**, **melts at higher temperatures**, so it withstands oven heat without deforming.

**Food bags: LD poly(ethene).** This is a **thermosoftening** polymer: its chains are separate and held by weak forces, so it is **flexible** — ideal for a bag that must fold. Because it **melts when heated**, it can also be **melted down and reshaped**, making it far easier to recycle than a thermosetting polymer, whose cross-links prevent remelting.

In each case the choice follows from the property the job demands: hardness for a blade, corrosion resistance for a sink, thermal stability for ovenware, and flexibility with recyclability for a bag.

examTechnique.body:
**Bronze is copper and tin; brass is copper and zinc.** Carats are **twenty-fourths**, so 18 carat is $\frac{18}{24} = 75\%$ gold. Steels vary with **carbon content**, and **chromium and nickel** make them stainless.

**Soda-lime glass** is sand, sodium carbonate and limestone; **borosilicate** is sand and boron trioxide and **melts higher**. **Thermosoftening melts; thermosetting does not**, because of **cross-links**. A **composite** is a **matrix** binding a **reinforcement**.
examinerErrors: Saying bronze is copper and zinc.
Treating a carat number as a percentage.
Attributing stainless steel to extra carbon rather than chromium and nickel.
Giving a use without the property that justifies it.
Saying LD and HD poly(ethene) come from different monomers.
Explaining thermosetting polymers without mentioning cross-links.
Describing a composite as simply a mixture.
Forgetting that both glasses start from sand.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names each alloy's composition precisely, gives a use **with the property that justifies it**, and converts carats by dividing by 24. It attributes stainless steel to **chromium and nickel**, explains borosilicate glass by its **higher melting temperature**, and distinguishes the two polymer types **structurally** — separate chains with weak forces against covalent **cross-links**. It knows LD and HD poly(ethene) differ by **conditions** rather than monomer, and identifies both the **matrix** and the **reinforcement** when describing a composite.
